400.e: The policy would hire private firms for military transport, supplies and equipment maintenance whenever their offers cost less. For example, a private firm could maintain military vehicles when its bid costs less than having the work done directly by public staff.
p: We support this approach to defence equipment because we value private initiative with clear responsibility: a service in defence equipment has a reason to improve when its income depends on customers returning. We are perfectly happy for a private factory to make a profit while making our tanks.

We oppose this approach to defence equipment. Leaving the bill entirely with customers can put defence equipment out of reach precisely when someone needs it most. That reflects our commitment to care that does not depend on personal wealth when judging defence equipment. We would like overseas aid to build a clinic before it builds an investor’s holiday home.

We would vote for this balance on defence equipment, guided by freedom to invest and choose a provider: defence manufacturers must attract willing customers rather than assume that taxpayers will meet the bill. Even an expensive tank deserves more than one price quote.

Our concern for security beyond being a profitable customer gives us a reason to reject this: in defence equipment, a real need can exist without the purchasing power required to make it profitable. We would like public investment to rebuild lives before it rebuilds anyone’s share price.

We oppose this approach to defence equipment because we value ordinary people having leverage over powerful providers: in defence equipment, a real need can exist without the purchasing power required to make it profitable. We would like rebuilding a country to produce homes before it produces another round of private bonuses.

For us, defence equipment must reflect enterprise within dependable public rules; we can back this because private finance puts the commercial risk of defence equipment on those choosing to invest their money. We would like a strong defence budget with at least one person still checking the invoice.

For us, an economy serving workers instead of owners is a reason to oppose this: in defence equipment, a real need can exist without the purchasing power required to make it profitable. We would like the people paying for national defence to own more than the bill.

The cheapest offer can conceal a dependence that becomes dangerous when equipment fails during a crisis. We put assured national capacity and a clear command above commercial savings, so military leaders must not be bound to outsource simply because a private bid appears less expensive. We prefer a chain of command with fewer people asking whether they are allowed to hold the chain.
